post1.text:
Hiring more executives does not solve a leadership problem. It multiplies it.

Companies scaling past $50M consistently make the same mistake: they treat leadership capacity as a headcount problem. Add a C-suite seat, fill it fast, assume the gap closes. It rarely does.

What actually drives scale is leadership architecture, not leadership volume. Three things matter more than how many executives you have:

1. Clarity of decision rights. Who owns what, fully, without ambiguity. At growth stage, overlapping authority is deadweight.

2. Leaders who build systems, not dependencies. If your company slows when a senior person travels, that is not a leadership team. That is a collection of individual contributors with titles.

3. Culture accountability at every layer. Alpha Compute's recent executive team expansion signals this directly: scaling infrastructure requires leaders who operate consistently without being watched.

The question is not whether you have enough leaders. It is whether the leaders you have are building something that outlasts their presence.

What does your leadership team look like when you are not in the room?

post2.text:
A recent piece in HousingWire covered Buffini and Company adding three senior executives specifically to scale their coaching business. That detail is worth pausing on.

They did not hire to maintain. They hired to scale. That distinction matters enormously for companies in the $50M to $500M range.

At Autobahn Consultants, we see this play out constantly. Leaders who confuse operational hires with growth hires stall out. The executive who keeps today running and the executive who builds tomorrow's capacity are rarely the same person. Knowing which one you need, and when, is one of the clearest signals of organizational maturity.

If you are building your senior team right now, ask yourself: am I hiring for where we are or where we need to be in 36 months?

Read the full article here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMicEFVX3lxTE80SmJLNXdFS1VDcE9QNXQ2YzNFUDNUSzItcWljNWEyb2NEUVJ0UzdweEIzaVZyclAyWk5fcW54Nlo2U21GSVVoMHFJaVpLSFdaMU1tMXRIWU8wMTJvc3RJNTM5VkhoaVFxZnZFM0VlWVU

post3.text:
When Buffini and Company brought on three senior executives to scale their coaching operation, they were making a leadership bet. That bet only pays off if those leaders know how to lead when the stakes are high and the pressure is constant.

Chapter 1 of Rock Your Business, titled Lead Like Lives Depend On It, was written by Katherine Slain precisely for this moment. The chapter confronts something most scaling companies avoid: the gap between being a capable leader and being the kind of leader a growing organization actually needs.

Katherine's insight is not about leadership style or personality. It is about what happens to your team when the pressure rises and the playbook runs out.

The companies that scale well do not just hire strong leaders. They build leaders who perform when it matters most.

post1.text:
Most business owners think about their exit too late. By the time they're ready to sell, they've already left millions on the table.

Here's the uncomfortable truth: your exit strategy should be built into how you run the business today, not assembled in a panic when you decide you're done.

Silicon Valley Bank recently outlined how the timing of a sale is rarely the primary driver of value. The business fundamentals you build over years determine what buyers will actually pay.

Three things $50M+ leaders consistently underestimate:

1. EBITDA margin improvement of even two points can dramatically shift your valuation multiple. Buyers pay for trajectory, not just current performance.

2. Customer concentration is a silent killer of deal value. If your top three clients represent 40% of revenue, sophisticated buyers will reprice the risk.

3. Management depth matters as much as financial performance. A business that runs without you is worth far more than one that depends on you.

So here is the real question: if a buyer walked in tomorrow, would your business command the multiple you believe it deserves?

post2.text:
A recent piece from J.P. Morgan Private Bank walks through the core business exit strategies available to owners, from strategic sales to private equity and family succession.

It is solid foundational content. But here is what it does not tell you: the strategy you choose matters far less than how prepared your business is when that moment arrives.

At Autobahn, we work with companies scaling from $50M toward $500M and beyond. The ones who exit on their terms share one trait: they treated their company as a sellable asset years before they ever intended to sell.

That discipline changes everything, from how they price contracts to how they build their leadership bench.

If you are in that growth window, now is exactly the right time to think about this. Read the J.P. Morgan piece here and then ask yourself whether your business is actually ready: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMitwFBVV95cUxOalJUT0c3NEFPTndZX08zeGN0dXVFOEJVcmVLRml0QUNjb2xXU3Nxd2ZjOW1mUVUtc0F6SDZ0M056b2Rpd21ZZWF6aVBpOHZESjRiMEtKYk13Sm52VTJJTzV5ZzhFVTE5LVVtcVN4aVpiUzJYUUEtclFONlM4S0NzS3owaFRDT3p6Z2NoZlhjSUh1QnhsWTkyT3pKQkJZR3YxWnZHSHpHTDQ3MEtSRDdBb1JDTVJrb1U

post3.text:
BDC recently published research showing that while most entrepreneurs feel personally ready to exit their businesses, very few have actually prepared the business itself for a transition.

That gap is exactly what Chapter 2 of our upcoming book addresses.

In 'Rock Your Business: Navigating the Road from $50 Million to $500 Million and Beyond,' chapter authors Paul Belair and George Hohman break down what it actually takes to maximize your valuation multiple before you ever sit across from a buyer.

The chapter is titled 'Maximize Your Multiple to Achieve Your Exit,' and one of its core findings will surprise a lot of operators: the moves that drive the highest multiples are rarely financial. They are structural, and they take time to build correctly.

If you are running a $50M business, the window to act is open right now.

post1.text:
Most strategic plans fail not because of bad strategy, but because leadership teams treat planning as an event instead of a system.

Research covered in Forbes confirms what we see constantly with scaling companies: the gap between strategy and execution is almost never a knowledge problem. It is a discipline and structure problem.

Here is what leaders of $50M+ businesses need to hear:

1. Your quarterly rhythm matters more than your annual plan. A plan that sits in a deck is not a plan. It is a wish list.

2. Accountability needs an owner, not a committee. Diffused ownership kills execution every time.

3. The companies that scale fastest are the ones that build a repeatable process for reviewing and adjusting strategy, not just setting it.

Strategy is not the hard part. Staying disciplined enough to execute it while your business is growing fast and pulling in every direction at once, that is the real challenge.

What is the single biggest thing that derails execution inside your organization?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Harvard Business School Online breaks down what actually makes strategy implementation work inside organizations, and it is worth your time if you lead a scaling business.

What stands out to us at Autobahn: the article reinforces something we see repeatedly with companies in the $50M to $500M range. Implementation does not collapse because the strategy was wrong. It collapses because the structure around execution was never built.

At that growth stage, you cannot rely on informal communication and good intentions. You need clear owners, defined milestones, and leadership alignment that goes beyond the executive team agreeing in a room.

If your strategy feels solid but results are lagging, the gap is almost always in execution infrastructure, not the plan itself.

Read the full piece here and think about where your own process breaks down: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiZ0FVX3lxTE5pcmMwWURjZ3NNYXZQOUI0V1Vwalk4TTJORHlsOEZOM2FlZG9ZSmw1LWFGc0RIYzNOcFNZbTkxRFhjWjdTdWkzek04UEhLblBJdWVUaGg2ZEsyeHJKd01YTXV6QXpTb2M

post3.text:
Strategic planning gets a lot of attention. Execution gets a lot of blame. But what actually connects the two?

In Chapter 3 of Rock Your Business, "What We Learned Selling Fish Food and Nike Shoes," authors Rafa Loyo and Jim Randall draw on experience across wildly different industries to answer exactly that question.

One of the sharpest insights in the chapter: the companies that execute well are not smarter or better resourced. They have learned to treat execution as its own discipline with its own process, separate from the work of building the strategy in the first place.

That distinction sounds simple. Most leadership teams at scaling companies have never actually made it.

If your plans keep outliving your follow-through, this chapter will hit close to home.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Most companies at $50M think their biggest sales problem is closing. It isn't. It's that they don't have a sales strategy at all.

They have a sales habit. A collection of relationships, gut instincts, and whatever worked last quarter. That's not a strategy. And at scale, it becomes a liability.

Recent research from McKinsey confirms what we see constantly with clients: B2B companies that hit a revenue ceiling aren't losing on price or product. They're losing because they can't replicate what made them successful in the first place. Growth starts requiring a system, not just hustle.

Here's what actually changes the trajectory:

1. Define who you are NOT selling to. Clarity on the wrong customer protects your margins.
2. Build a repeatable motion before you hire more salespeople. Headcount without process is expensive noise.
3. Treat your sales strategy as a living document reviewed quarterly, not an annual slide deck.

So here's the question: If your top salesperson left tomorrow, would your revenue follow them out the door?

post2.text:
A recent piece from Bain and Company caught our attention. Their research on the B2B growth divide shows a clear and uncomfortable split: a small group of companies is pulling away from the pack, and the gap is widening fast. The differentiator isn't budget or brand. It's how intentionally they go to market.

For companies scaling from $50M to $500M, this isn't abstract. It's urgent. The window where you can grow on relationships and referrals alone closes faster than most leaders expect.

At Autobahn, we work with leadership teams every day who are still running $20M sales habits inside a $70M business. That mismatch is expensive and fixable, but only if you name it first.

Read the Bain piece and then ask yourself honestly: which side of that divide are you on?

The title of Chapter 4 in our upcoming book says it plainly: Every Day Without a Real Sales Strategy is a Donation.

Chapter authors Deb and Brandon wrote it that way on purpose. Because that's exactly what's happening inside most companies at the $50M to $100M mark. Revenue is coming in, but without a deliberate strategy behind it, a portion of every dollar is walking out the door uncaptured.

post1.text:
Your brand is not your logo. It is not your tagline. It is the feeling someone gets when they walk away from an interaction with your company.

Most $50M+ businesses obsess over visual identity and completely ignore sensory experience. That is a costly mistake.

Campari's approach to brand stewardship, covered recently in Adweek, makes this point well. They have maintained relevance across generations not by chasing trends but by anchoring everything to a consistent emotional core that customers can recognize before they even read the label.

Here is what scaling companies miss:

1. Customers form brand impressions in seconds. Inconsistency at any touchpoint erodes the trust you spent years building.
2. Culture and brand are not separate conversations. What your team believes internally shows up externally without fail.
3. Brand investment without measurement is just spending. Tie every brand decision to a business outcome.

If a new customer experienced only your marketing for 60 seconds, what would they feel? And would your best customers agree with that answer?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Adweek on how Campari manages its portfolio of iconic brands raises a question every scaling company should sit with: are you actively managing your brand, or just maintaining it?

There is a difference. Maintenance is reactive. Management is intentional.

For companies growing through the $50M to $500M range, brand drift is a real and underestimated risk. As you add products, markets, and team members, the original clarity of what you stand for gets diluted. Fast.

The companies that scale well treat brand as a strategic asset with an owner, a process, and regular review. Not just a creative exercise.

If your brand strategy has not been pressure-tested in the last 12 months, that is where to start.

Read the full piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiuwFBVV95cUxOME5NSGZueEQtNEplYmN2bWt2NHBnYWlPNEM3Wm5JYnhlMzNxSGpiRkxhN1NmVVh2UnVFa0dXTG1rNFA3d05RdkRNcUkxcGlaMVRSTklhZDFpVkttRVN1SFFGY2lVRDRncTQ3WXQwYkx3NW55MHdiTGlYVlN0ZXBJa0NtYjVCa21FOFF6eFNFYVZPcVFyTk91OG5rZ2FRX1M0MnNvalZFQW1PVXBUZDJIcmFaSlMtUFJkVFZz

post3.text:
Ulta's CMO recently spoke with Marketing Dive about the challenge of building a brand while also driving performance across every sales channel. It is a tension most growing companies know well and few resolve cleanly.

Chapter 5 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, tackles this head-on. The chapter is called "What Does Your Marketing Smell Like?" and it was written by Kayli Simpson and Yasmin West.

The title is intentional. Kayli and Yasmin argue that your brand has a sensory signature, something customers experience before they consciously process it. And for companies scaling past $50M, getting that signature right is not a creative luxury. It is a growth lever.

They share a framework for making that tangible and actionable, even inside complex, fast-moving organizations.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Hiring more people faster is not a growth strategy. It is a liability strategy.

Most companies scaling past $50M treat talent acquisition like a volume game. Post more roles, interview more candidates, fill seats quickly. Then they wonder why culture erodes, performance dips, and turnover spikes two quarters later.

SHRM's recent research on hiring in 2026 makes this plain: the companies winning on talent are shifting from scale to precision. They are defining exactly what a role needs to produce before the first resume lands on a desk.

Three things high-growth companies do differently:

1. They write outcome-based role definitions, not job descriptions.
2. They measure quality of hire 90 days in, not just time to fill.
3. They treat every bad hire as a process failure, not a people failure.

Your hiring process is either a filter or a funnel. Only one of those produces a team that can carry you to $500M.

Which one are you running right now?

post2.text:
A recent piece in UC Today made a point that every scaling company needs to hear: your HR platform does not fix broken hiring, it amplifies it.

If your process is selecting the wrong people, automation and AI just get you to the wrong people faster and at greater volume.

For companies growing from $50M toward $500M, this is not a software problem. It is a strategy problem. The tools you layer on top of a flawed talent model will not save you. They will bury you in a bigger pile of the same mistakes.

Before your next platform upgrade or AI integration, audit the fundamentals. Who owns the hiring standard? What does a great hire actually look like for your stage of growth?

Get the process right first. Then scale it.

Read the full article here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiqgFBVV95cUxQWjRQeU5RQWw1SlRfNElDUmhDVDFNUDBXeTE1NlJUOVI2TmVTVGY0aVpTVDJXYlh2bm1PWXhFUkFVZFZQT2tfWDQxMFowcm5jWWRLWlpPNFp5bUJyMXlhdnR5NkxXWTBVWGFzTDVDaGVNYnZEVjRxSEVSQW9jVmZzbGVyTjYwSzZBUTd0LWtvWWlyOEk5Qmg5bEduaHRuVTNTdUhqVDhETGFtZw?oc=5

post3.text:
SHRM's recent findings on precision hiring in 2026 land squarely on something Chapter 6 of Rock Your Business addresses head on.

The chapter is called The Talent Engine, written by Caleb Hawkins, Darla Klein, and Yasmin West. It was built for leaders navigating the stretch from $50M to $500M, where the talent decisions you make today determine whether your infrastructure holds or cracks under growth.

One thing the chapter makes clear: the companies that struggle to scale are almost never short on people. They are short on the right people in the right roles with the right clarity around what success looks like.

Precision is not a recruiting tactic. It is an organizational discipline.

There is a framework in this chapter that changes how leadership teams think about building that discipline. We will be sharing more soon.

post1.text:
More KPIs do not make better companies. They make distracted ones.

Most leadership teams at the $50M to $500M stage fall into the same trap: they add metrics every quarter and never subtract any. The dashboard grows. Clarity shrinks. And the people responsible for hitting numbers stop understanding which numbers actually matter.

Harvard Business School recently outlined how a focused set of marketing KPIs, tracked with discipline, produces sharper decisions than broad measurement ever can. The same logic applies across every function in a scaling business.

Here is what high-growth leaders should take seriously:

First, if your team cannot recite their top three metrics from memory, you have too many. Second, a KPI that does not connect to a specific decision is just data decoration. Third, the right metrics at $50M are almost never the right metrics at $200M. Your measurement strategy has to scale with your business model.

So ask yourself: when did your company last retire a KPI?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Business.com highlights 14 tools companies can use to track KPIs. Solid list. But here is what that article does not address: tool selection is not the problem for most scaling companies. Metric selection is.

At Autobahn, we work with businesses in the $50M to $500M range, and the pattern is consistent. Leaders invest in better dashboards before they agree on what the dashboards should show. The result is expensive software displaying the wrong information with beautiful precision.

Before you evaluate another tracking tool, get your leadership team aligned on which five to seven numbers genuinely drive your business forward. The right tool serving the right metrics will outperform any enterprise platform pointed at the wrong ones.

Read the full article and then ask the harder question: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMingFBVV95cUxQcWNPSTVTUDVYYURoVkZKa0ItNEtQbmJqWlNJTlIzUVZqclAxMHFaajNobC1JbGNkZGZVajN6MWJLT1pJcXktVG10VG8zUUljdU43NU5WR1cyNDB4QkxONlJkb3hJR2FfNzdGZHd1VWhPbTktdU1vdTEzamFWY2ZFVDNKUFIwRG91ZDdWU1UyN2twNFpLd1JjU3EzTUpjdw?oc=5

post3.text:
Everyone talks about tracking the right KPIs. Very few companies actually do it.

Chapter 7 of our upcoming book, "Rock Your Business: Navigating the Road from $50 Million to $500 Million and Beyond," takes that problem head on. Titled "Death by KPIs," the chapter was authored by Hector Arias, Matt Radicelli, and Jim Randall, three practitioners who have watched growing companies drown in their own data.

One of the sharpest insights in the chapter is this: the volume of metrics a company tracks often moves inversely with how well the team understands performance. More measurement is not more accountability. It is more noise.

The authors lay out a framework for identifying which numbers deserve attention at each stage of growth, and which ones are quietly wasting your team's time.

post1.text:
Most executives think AI adoption is going well. Their employees disagree. That gap is not a morale problem. It is a strategy problem.

A recent New York Times investigation found a sharp disconnect between how leaders perceive AI rollouts and how frontline employees actually experience them. That disconnect has real costs for companies trying to scale.

Here is what business leaders at the $50M+ level need to understand:

1. Productivity gains from AI are real, but they do not distribute themselves. Someone has to architect how AI enters the workflow, or it creates confusion instead of capacity.

2. The executives who see AI as a productivity win are right, but only when implementation is intentional. Without clear ownership, AI tools become expensive noise.

3. The companies scaling fastest are treating AI adoption like an operational initiative, not an IT project. That means accountability, training, and measurement from the top down.

You cannot lead a transformation you do not understand. So here is the real question: how close are you to what your team actually experiences with AI every day?

post2.text:
A recent piece in The New York Times uncovered something that should concern every growth-stage CEO: leaders believe their AI rollouts are succeeding while employees are quietly struggling with the reality on the ground.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern constantly in companies scaling from $50M to $500M. Leadership sets the vision, announces the tools, and assumes adoption follows. It rarely does.

The gap between executive optimism and employee experience is not a people problem. It is a systems problem. Scaling companies need a deliberate structure for how AI integrates into daily work, who owns that integration, and how results are measured.

If your AI strategy lives in a slide deck and not in your operating rhythm, you are already behind.

Read the full piece and think about where your own gaps might be: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMivwFBVV95cUxQWWdVcmp6Vm8xaTlHbXhmRUp2bnU1Q2hlMUY1eG05ekVJSWFPRjRZWGcyODNDeUV4dW5IUndhM2NtWlJDSE1QSmhlekNNVUotb2NHRjBwRTc4dkR0Y3RNeUIwWlZNUk1hOTc2dEJYTEVUUlVhSXFmeUx1RlZWNjJ0ZmhINTRHcXZac0NtOUd2RE9oTUU1Rk9TLWJmSlpFTWxfaVlSdUhkZ2p3ZVB3LXhWSVZSS004ZkNzRlFWUzVjVQ?oc=5

post3.text:
The disconnect between how executives and employees experience AI is not new to us. It is exactly why Chapter 8 of Rock Your Business exists.

Chapter 8, The Third Monitor Theory, written by Hudson Shank and Jonathan Slain, tackles the specific challenge that scaling companies face when AI enters the building without a real framework behind it. The chapter gets its name from a simple but powerful concept about how leaders at high-growth companies should be thinking about AI as a dedicated layer of their operating system, not an add-on.

Most companies at the $50M to $500M stage are using AI reactively. The Third Monitor Theory gives you a structure for using it strategically, in a way your whole organization can actually follow.

The gap the New York Times identified is real. This chapter helps you close it.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

The problem is not the technology. It is the absence of a deliberate framework for making AI operational at every level of the business. Here is what leaders between $50M and $500M need to get right before the gap becomes a chasm.

post1.text:
The leaders most likely to destroy their companies are the ones who never doubt themselves.

Imposter syndrome gets treated like a problem to solve. For leaders scaling a business past $50M, it is actually a signal worth paying attention to.

A recent Campaign US piece made the case that imposter syndrome should be put to work rather than eliminated. That framing matters. Here is why it applies to growth-stage companies specifically.

First, self-doubt at scale forces due diligence. Leaders who question their own assumptions ask better questions of their teams and their data. Second, the discomfort of feeling out of your depth is often accurate feedback. Your company has changed. Your role needs to change with it. Third, leaders who have made peace with uncertainty make faster decisions under pressure. They are not waiting to feel certain before they act.

The goal is not to silence the doubt. The goal is to stop letting it drive.

What has imposter syndrome actually taught you about how you lead?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Campaign US argued that leaders should stop trying to outgrow imposter syndrome and start putting it to work instead.

For companies scaling from $50M toward $500M, that reframe is not just useful, it is urgent.

At that stage, the game changes fast. New markets, new org structures, new competitors. Leaders who have always relied on certainty before acting will stall. The ones who learn to move with doubt as a passenger, not a driver, tend to build the organizations that actually make it through.

Imposter syndrome is not a character flaw. At scale, it is often a sign that you are paying close attention to how much harder the road ahead actually is.

Read the full piece here and think about where this shows up in your own leadership: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMikgFBVV95cUxNS0JPUmJPTk9IMzNvR21BSC03djE4MDZhVko0eFNpaDZnUzl4MnpTUTBfVFJacUZrNm8tNm5KYXdIUmtwR0FVN0trR2lwcHVFQ3ZIZlJORUJZcUo3VUtnOGhycm1pcmY3WGh5ckQxU1NrU1cyc01PbllsblhxSTAzUzA0bkRheUthNkhhSXl5Sjd1dw?oc=5

post3.text:
How could you be successful and not have it?

That is the question at the center of Chapter 9 in our upcoming book, Rock Your Business: Navigating the Road from $50 Million to $500 Million and Beyond.

Chapter co-author Samantha Frost and her co-authors dig into something most leadership books gloss over: imposter syndrome does not go away when you hit a revenue milestone. For many leaders, it gets louder. And the companies that scale well tend to be led by people who have figured out what to do with that noise.

The chapter does not offer a checklist for feeling more confident. It offers something more useful: a way to understand what the doubt is actually telling you about your leadership and your organization.

If you lead a growth-stage company, this chapter is going to hit close to home.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Every leader who has scaled a company past $50M knows the feeling: the revenue is real, the team is growing, and somehow you still wonder if you are the right person to be in the room. Imposter syndrome at the growth stage is not a confidence problem. It is a signal. The leaders who learn to read it correctly build companies that last. The ones who ignore it, or let it paralyze them, do not.

post1.text:
The most dangerous myth in business is that work-life balance is something you earn after you scale.

It is not a reward. It is a requirement.

Deutsche Bank's wealth planning research on founders makes this clear: entrepreneurs who fail to build intentional life structures alongside their business structures consistently underperform in both categories long-term. The separation between the person and the company never happens by accident.

Here is what leaders scaling past $50M rarely hear:

First, your calendar is your life plan. If it is not on the schedule, it does not exist. Second, the decisions that protect your personal life are the same muscle you use to protect your business margins. Both require saying no. Third, burnout at the $100M stage is not a motivation problem. It is a design problem.

Most founders optimize the business architecture relentlessly and leave their personal architecture completely to chance.

What would it look like if you applied the same rigor to designing your life that you apply to designing your company?

post2.text:
A recent piece from Deutsche Bank Wealth Management on planning for entrepreneurs and startup founders raises something scaling companies often ignore until it is too late: the financial and personal architecture of the founder rarely keeps pace with the business.

At Autobahn, we see this constantly. A company crosses $50M, the operational complexity multiplies, and the leader's personal plan is still built for the version of their life from five years ago.

Wealth planning is not just a finance conversation. It is a leadership sustainability conversation. The clearer a founder is on where they are going personally, the better decisions they make professionally.

If your business plan is more detailed than your life plan, that is worth fixing now, not later.

Read the full piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMisAFBVV95cUxQOTFRM1pIdEtXSndlcGN4blIxdlc3RHVLVmRuTkRGTFlzTU91X1YzZzNfTk9YNmtHS3psaHlFX3I1V3JWR2NYYzFpQ1NPazIzWFVHaTlRNHFFUFVLTHJJQkZMV1RwX3BOaWhzNTZjRmlMUXBhMHhuNHdKUFJOSEtINko4YnpWQ0FWYWozY0Iza2JJVzh3NGg2UjYtM0F4RDRZR25zbXN0Ykd6TG9qOV9FcA

post3.text:
Wealth planning for entrepreneurs is a timely topic. But Deutsche Bank's recent piece on founder financial planning only tells half the story.

The other half is what Chapter 10 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, tackles directly.

The chapter is called Coming Up for Air. Authors Samantha Frost, Jonathan Slain, and Katherine Slain wrote it because scaling leaders consistently tell us the same thing: they built a company they are proud of and a life they barely recognize.

One insight from that chapter that reframes everything: life planning is not something you do alongside your business plan. It is a prerequisite for the business plan actually working at scale.

The structure you build for your personal life determines the ceiling for your professional performance. Full stop.

posts.blog_hook: Most scaling leaders have a five-year business plan and a zero-year life plan. At $50M and beyond, that gap stops being manageable and starts being dangerous. The founders who successfully reach $500M are not better operators. They are better designers of the whole picture, business and life together. Here is what that actually looks like in practice.
